analysis.title: CIO Special: 10 themes for the year ahead
key_insights: Theme 1: DWS expects US-Europe friction under Trump to end in a stronger, more balanced alliance rather than a break. It points to Brexit, which advertised the cost of leaving, and to deep financial ties: about 60% of US foreign direct investment goes to Europe and a similar share flows the other way.

Theme 2: Emerging and developing economies are 61% of global GDP on a PPP basis, and the IMF expects 3.8% growth for them in 2026 against 1.7% for advanced economies. DWS says strong GDP growth does not guarantee strong equity returns. It favors country and sector selection over broad EM exposure and notes tight India renewable credit spreads favor carry over valuation upside.

Theme 3: Under Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, DWS expects the Fed to be less quick to step in, with fiscal policy getting more attention. The open question is where yields settle long term. Elevated deficits, issuance and term premium may keep yields above 2010s levels, with the 30-year Treasury yield at a multi-decade high of 5.5%. High-valuation, long-duration assets look most vulnerable. Stable cash flow, strong balance sheets and pricing power look more resilient, and credit dispersion should widen.

Theme 3 (what matters): DWS says the cause of higher yields decides the damage. Yields rising on stronger growth are absorbable. Yields rising on deficits, inflation and term premium raise pressure on consumers, businesses and valuations. Warsh specifically called out record new issuance, demand and tight credit spreads.

Theme 4: Germany's Altersvorsorgedepot, a state-supported retirement account without a capital guarantee, starts in 2027 and opens ETFs and funds to savers. A second proposal from the Pension Commission would add a capital-funded pillar with 2% extra contributions, about 35 billion euros a year. Germany is over 4% of global output but only about 1% of global pension assets.

Theme 5: DWS is constructive on European equities. The S&P 500's ten largest names are nearly 40% of the index, about twice the Stoxx Europe 600 top-ten share, and tech is over 50% of S&P 500 earnings. DWS splits Europe into 'New Europe' (industrials, banks, semiconductors, utilities, now about 40% of the Stoxx 600 versus about 25% in 2015) and 'Old Europe' (autos, chemicals, consumer goods). It expects average European earnings growth to return to double digits in 2026 and 2027 after three years of stagnation.

Theme 5 (AI angle): Europe could gain from broader AI adoption across industry rather than from building AI platforms. About one in seven Stoxx 600 companies already benefits from AI investment. German reform and defense and strategic-autonomy spending are further supports, and 55% of Stoxx 600 revenue comes from outside Europe.

Theme 6: AI agents are driving token usage and compute demand, and the focus is shifting from investment to monetization. Chipmakers sit at a supply bottleneck, earn higher margins and are expected to see sharply rising free cash flow through 2028. Hyperscalers are moving from asset-light to capital-intensive and increasingly rely on external financing. DWS says to worry about returns, not demand.

Theme 6 (leadership): With agentic AI, DWS expects tech leadership to broaden beyond semiconductors toward cloud, software and cybersecurity. It notes semiconductor-heavy indices fell more than 20% from June peaks by October 2026, with the SOX down 24% and the KOSPI down 39% as of 10/19/26. Valuation and timing matter even if chipmakers enter their most profitable years.

Theme 7: Concentration is high. The top market-cap decile was 78% of US equity value in July 2026 while the number of companies in it fell to 165. DWS lists four AI risks: spending may not earn enough revenue, valuations depend on demanding profit forecasts, the buildout may raise financing costs, and today's winners may not be the lasting beneficiaries.

Theme 7 (response): DWS recommends diversifying within the AI ecosystem, between financiers of spending and firms whose earnings depend on it. It also suggests AI-linked but independent drivers (grid, automation, cybersecurity), non-AI earnings drivers (financials, health care, defense, selected small and mid caps), government bonds against a disinflationary shock, and energy and real assets against an inflationary one. Buying foreign firms exposed to the same AI cycle adds little diversification.

Theme 8: US population growth is at its lowest in more than a century, so growth depends more on productivity. DWS sees industrial, service-oriented retail and higher-quality residential property as relatively well positioned. Conventional offices outside the prime segment face structural pressure. Renting has regained a cost advantage over buying.

Theme 9: Water is becoming a constraint on trade, industry and growth. Data centers, chip fabs and critical-mineral mining are water-intensive, often in water-stressed regions such as Arizona. DWS expects water to be repriced and sees two opportunity sets: risk identification in water-intensive sectors (utilities, chemicals, food) and solutions (treatment, recycling, leakage reduction, desalination, precision irrigation).

Theme 10: Falling launch costs and reusable rockets could make space an infrastructure layer for communications, data and Earth observation. The beneficiary set is wider than rocket makers: satellite operators, data analytics, defense, semiconductors and energy-technology firms. Orbital data centers and in-space manufacturing are more likely 2030s and 2040s stories, and DWS says investors should stay selective.
Closing message: DWS names broad diversification as the best protection against severe losses from uncertainty.

sector_views.sector: European industrials, banks, semiconductors and utilities (New Europe)
sector_views.rationale: Structural drivers of electrification, defense, infrastructure and financial-sector consolidation. These sectors have grown earnings faster than autos, chemicals and consumer goods.
Bottleneck position gives high margins and rising free cash flow, but forward multiples depend on earnings delivery and the group fell over 20% from its June peak.
Free cash flow is under pressure from capex and reliance on external financing, which DWS says could prove temporary if AI and cloud revenue justifies the spend.
DWS expects tech leadership to broaden toward the application layer as agentic AI spreads.
Slower working-age population growth and AI reshaping office jobs limit demand.

sector_views.sector: US industrial, service-oriented retail and higher-quality residential real estate
sector_views.rationale: E-commerce logistics demand, data-center related demand, service tenants and a rent-versus-buy cost advantage.
Non-discretionary demand for treatment, recycling and leakage reduction may be more durable and less cyclical.

earnings_insights: DWS expects average European earnings growth to return to double digits in 2026 and 2027 after three years of stagnation (DWS forecast, not a reported figure).

Consensus estimates (not reported figures) point to a sharp rise in semiconductor free cash flow through 2028, while hyperscaler free cash flow lags, per DWS's chart of five chipmakers (Nvidia, TSMC, Broadcom, Micron, AMD) against five hyperscalers (Alphabet, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, Oracle).

Technology companies account for more than 50% of S&P 500 earnings, and forward 12-month S&P 500 earnings are nearly 90% above the cyclically adjusted earnings base, which DWS says leaves forward multiples dependent on exceptional earnings growth.

Only about three in ten large S&P 500 and FTSE 100 companies could point to at least one realised, quantified AI result, per an AI Value Gap analysis cited by DWS (Q2 2026 data, about 15% of the sample yet to report).

macro_indicators.indicator: Emerging and developing economies real GDP growth
macro_indicators.interpretation: IMF July 2026 forecast, versus 1.7% for advanced economies. DWS uses it to argue EM remains the growth engine but says selectivity matters.
IMF July 2026 forecast, the comparison base for EM growth.
Chart annotation. DWS says elevated deficits, issuance and term premium may keep long yields above 2010s levels.
DWS expects a rebound after three years of stagnation, mostly from New Europe sectors.
Modest because of demographics, which makes the foreign revenue share of European companies more important.

risk_factors: AI investment may not generate enough revenue or productivity to justify its cost, and AI may transform the economy without every involved company earning attractive shareholder returns.
Semiconductor valuations look affordable on forward multiples but become expensive if earnings disappoint.
AI buildout competes for a finite pool of capital and could raise financing costs for tech companies, utilities and suppliers, favoring those with stronger balance sheets.
Today's perceived AI winners may not be the lasting beneficiaries.
Higher yields driven by deficits, inflation and term premium could pressure consumers, businesses and valuations, and tighter financial conditions could undermine the capital-intensive AI cycle.
Hyperscalers' growing reliance on debt, with rising credit-default-swap spreads for lower-rated names, and new interdependencies if stronger firms back weaker ones.
Supplier exposure to hyperscaler capex, since hyperscalers can cut spending if returns weaken while concentrated suppliers have less flexibility.
Geopolitical uncertainty from the Iran conflict, tariffs and shifting alliances.
Emerging-market selectivity risk: political stability, regulation and capital-market maturity differ widely, and tight India credit spreads favor carry over valuation upside.
Water scarcity could curtail or strand facilities in water-stressed basins, such as chip fabs and data centers.
Space business models depend on reliable reusable rockets, funding and regulatory approvals, and many are 2030s to 2040s stories.
charts_described: US direct investment position by region in 2025 (USD billion): foreign direct investment in the US from Europe 4,300 versus US direct investment abroad in Europe 3,729, with Asia-Pacific 1,188 versus 1,108 and Canada 488 versus 747.
30-year US Treasury yield against US debt as a share of GDP (historical and CBO projection), with the 5.5% yield annotated as a multi-decade high.
Water withdrawn during electricity generation (liters per MWh): wind under 10, solar PV 100, gas CCGT 750, coal 2,540, nuclear 2,600.
AI build-out free cash flow chart (USD bn, 2015 to 2028E) comparing five semiconductor companies with five hyperscalers, with semiconductor free cash flow forecast to rise sharply.
Rent-to-mortgage payment ratio since 1996 against its 20-year and 30-year averages, with DWS saying renting has regained a clear cost advantage.
vol_and_positioning: US equity concentration: the top market-cap decile was 78% of US equity value in July 2026, close to the upper end of its long-run range, with only 165 companies in it.
The S&P 500's ten largest constituents are nearly 40% of the index, about twice the Stoxx Europe 600 top-ten share. Three of the ten are cyclical semiconductor companies.
Semiconductor-heavy indices fell more than 20% from their June peaks by October 2026 (SOX down 24%, KOSPI down 39% as of 10/19/26).
geopolitical: The US attack on Iran in February raised energy costs and inflation and lifted interest rates globally. The US administration's course and exit from the conflict remain unclear.
US tariffs can be announced with little lead time, and markets have adjusted to that.
Transatlantic tensions under Trump's America First policy, with DWS expecting a rebalancing of responsibilities and a stronger alliance rather than separation.
Europe's dependence on resources and its push for strategic autonomy, with rising public investment in defense.
A shift in global centers of power and alliances, including which major power emerging markets orient toward.
US-China technology competition expected to accelerate investment in space infrastructure, communications, defense and computing.
Supply disruptions from water stress, including Panama shipping, Colorado River pressure and European droughts.
cross_bank_references: BofA Global Research is cited for the Stoxx Europe 600 AI-exposure statistic (European Equity Strategy, 6/26/26) and for the launch-cost chart in the space theme.

tension_points.bull_case: AI agents are driving token usage and compute demand, chipmakers sit at a supply bottleneck with sharply rising consensus free cash flow through 2028, and H100 rental rates stayed near higher levels in June 2026.
tension_points.bear_case: Hyperscalers are shifting to capital-intensive models reliant on external financing, forward semiconductor multiples depend on exceptional earnings, and semiconductor-heavy indices are down more than 20% from their June peaks.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Semiconductor earnings disappointing against demanding forecasts, which DWS says would turn affordable-looking forward multiples into expensive ones.

tension_points.bull_case: Markets have shown they can absorb higher yields, and AI productivity gains could offset part of the rise in capital costs.
tension_points.bear_case: Deficits, heavy issuance and a higher term premium may keep long yields elevated, pressuring consumers, weaker borrowers, long-duration assets and the capital-intensive AI cycle.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Yields rising because of larger deficits, inflation and a higher term premium rather than stronger growth, which DWS says would raise pressure on consumers, businesses and valuations significantly.

theme_stances.key_argument: Companies at AI supply-chain bottlenecks, especially chipmakers, earn higher margins and free cash flow, while hyperscalers' financial position weakens.
theme_stances.evidence: those sitting at bottlenecks will tend to have higher margins

theme_stances.key_argument: Under Chair Warsh the Fed is less likely to step in outside severe crises, and yields may settle above 2010s levels.
theme_stances.evidence: Under the new Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, those days may be numbered

theme_stances.key_argument: European market structure is shifting toward higher-margin, structurally driven sectors such as industrials, banks, semiconductors and utilities.
theme_stances.evidence: Europe has no reason to hide
